title: UDP, QUIC and reliability trade-offs
scopeHtml:
Scope: UDP, QUIC, reliability trade-offs, MTU and fragmentation.

Scope: UDP, QUIC, reliability trade-offs, MTU and fragmentation.

notes.title: What UDP is
notes.html:
UDP sends independent messages (datagrams) with almost no extras: no connection, no ordering, no retransmission, no congestion control. The header is just 8 bytes: source port, destination port, length, checksum.

 0      7 8     15 16    23 24    31
+--------+--------+--------+--------+
|   Source Port   |  Destination Port|
+--------+--------+--------+--------+
|     Length      |     Checksum     |
+--------+--------+--------+--------+

A datagram arrives whole or not at all (the checksum catches corruption; message boundaries are preserved, unlike TCP). It may be lost, duplicated or reordered, and the application decides what to do.

# Quick UDP test with netcat
nc -u -l 9999                      # receiver
echo "hello" | nc -u 127.0.0.1 9999
sudo tcpdump -nn -i lo udp port 9999
# IP 127.0.0.1.54321 > 127.0.0.1.9999: UDP, length 6
ss -uln                            # listening UDP sockets

Worked example. Sending 100 bytes of game state 60 times a second: TCP adds a handshake and retransmits an old position when a newer one is already coming (head-of-line blocking). UDP's 8 + 20 + 100 = 128 bytes per packet and a lost packet is simply replaced by the next. Max UDP payload is 65,507 bytes (65,535 - 20 - 8) but real packets should stay below the MTU.

Industry examples. DNS (port 53), DHCP (67/68), NTP (123), SNMP, syslog, VoIP (RTP), video calls (WebRTC), online games, QUIC / HTTP/3 (UDP 443), WireGuard VPN (UDP 51820), mDNS, StatsD metrics.

Everyday analogy. Throwing postcards in a postbox: cheap and fast, no confirmation, some may never arrive.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying UDP is "unreliable so nobody uses it". It is the base for HTTP/3.
  • Believing UDP is faster on the wire. It just skips work; the same links and latencies apply.
  • Forgetting UDP has no congestion control, so a careless sender can flood the link.

notes.title: When to choose TCP, UDP or something else
notes.html:
Choose by what the application can tolerate.

Need Pick Why
Every byte, in order (files, DB, APIs) TCP built in
Latest state matters, old data is useless (games, telemetry, live video) UDP no head-of-line blocking
One tiny request/response (DNS) UDP avoids handshake
Multiplexed streams, mobile, fast connect QUIC independent streams, 0/1 RTT
Broadcast/multicast discovery UDP TCP is point to point
Reliable messaging with custom rules UDP + own protocol e.g. ENet, Aeron, KCP

Decision gravity. Building reliability over UDP yourself is a one-way door in complexity: you must reimplement ACKs, retransmit, congestion control and fairness, and get it wrong in public (a flooding sender hurts others). Prefer QUIC or an established library unless you have a proven need. Moving from TCP to QUIC is reversible if you keep TCP fallback (clients do try both).

Worked example. Video call at 30 fps: a frame taking 200 ms to retransmit arrives too late to display. Better to drop it and use the next frame or send forward error correction (FEC), costing e.g. 20% extra bandwidth to survive ~10% random loss with no retransmits.

Industry examples. Zoom/Meet/Teams use RTP over UDP with FEC and adaptive bitrate; Riot's and Valve's games send state snapshots over UDP; Cloudflare WARP and Tailscale use WireGuard over UDP; Kafka and databases stay on TCP.

Everyday analogy. A live sports commentary: if you miss a sentence, the commentator does not repeat it; they move on to what is happening now. A legal contract, by contrast, needs every clause.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "use UDP for speed" without stating the freshness-over-completeness reason.
  • Not mentioning that UDP is often blocked or rate-limited by corporate firewalls, so a TCP/TLS fallback is needed.

notes.title: MTU, MSS and fragmentation
notes.html:
MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) is the largest IP packet a link can carry; Ethernet is typically 1,500 bytes. MSS (Maximum Segment Size) is the largest TCP payload: MTU - 20 (IP) - 20 (TCP) = 1,460 (minus 12 more if timestamps are used, so 1,448).

If an IP packet is larger than the link MTU, IPv4 routers may fragment it into pieces that the destination reassembles. Fragmentation is bad: losing one fragment loses the whole datagram, reassembly costs CPU and memory, firewalls often drop fragments, and attackers abuse them.

Modern practice: set the DF (Don't Fragment) bit and use Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD): if a packet is too big, the router drops it and returns ICMP "Fragmentation needed" (type 3 code 4) with the next-hop MTU; the sender shrinks its packets. IPv6 routers never fragment; only the sender can.

Link MTUs along a path: 1500 -- 1500 -- 1400 (VPN) -- 1500
Sender sends 1500 B with DF -> router at 1400 drops, ICMP "need frag, mtu 1400" -> sender resends 1400 B packets
ip link show eth0                       # mtu 1500
ping -M do -s 1472 example.com          # Linux: DF set, 1472 + 28 header = 1500
# ping: local error: message too long, mtu=1400   <- shows the real path MTU
tracepath example.com                   # reports pmtu per hop
sudo tcpdump -nn 'icmp[0] == 3 and icmp[1] == 4'   # frag-needed messages

On Windows: ping -f -l 1472 example.com.

PMTUD black hole (a classic production incident). A firewall blocks all ICMP, so the "need frag" message never arrives. Small packets (the TCP handshake, small HTTP requests) work, but large responses hang forever, often exactly when TLS certificates or big POSTs are sent. Symptoms: connection connects, then stalls on large transfer; works on one network but not another. Fixes: allow ICMP type 3 code 4 (and IPv6 ICMPv6 packet-too-big), clamp MSS (iptables -t mangle -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu), or enable TCP MTU probing (net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing=1).

Typical MTUs. Ethernet 1,500; PPPoE (some DSL) 1,492; IPsec/OpenVPN tunnels about 1,400 to 1,440; WireGuard default 1,420; Jumbo frames 9,000 inside data centers (AWS supports 9,001 within a VPC, but internet-bound traffic stays at 1,500); Docker/Kubernetes overlays (VXLAN adds 50 bytes) often 1,450.

Worked example. Kubernetes pods using VXLAN on a 1,500 B network must use pod MTU 1,450 (1,500 - 50). If left at 1,500, large packets get dropped or fragmented, so a service works on curl but hangs for large JSON responses.

Industry examples. Cloudflare's published fragmentation work and the DNS flag day 2020 (EDNS buffer size 1232) were driven by fragmentation problems: DNS UDP answers are kept under ~1,232 bytes to avoid fragmenting. QUIC picks a conservative 1,200-byte minimum datagram size for the same reason.

Decision gravity. Raising MTU to jumbo inside a data center cuts CPU (fewer packets, ~6x fewer for bulk) but one mismatched device breaks things silently: all-or-nothing across the path. Lowering MTU/MSS clamp is a safe, reversible workaround.

Everyday analogy. Moving a sofa through doors of different widths: you find the narrowest door by trying (PMTUD) or you cut the sofa into pieces (fragmentation) and hope no piece is lost.

Common interview traps.

  • Dropping all ICMP at the firewall "for security". It breaks PMTUD.
  • Mixing up MTU (IP packet) and MSS (TCP payload).
  • Forgetting tunnels and overlays shrink the usable MTU.

notes.title: Building reliability on UDP
notes.html:
If you need some reliability but not TCP's rules, you add pieces yourself. What TCP bundles, and the UDP-world alternative:

Feature How you add it over UDP
Ordering sequence numbers, reorder buffer (jitter buffer in VoIP)
Loss recovery ACK/NACK + selective retransmit, or FEC (Reed-Solomon, XOR parity)
Congestion control you must implement one (NewReno, CUBIC, BBR, GCC for WebRTC)
Flow control window or credit scheme
Connection identity connection IDs, handshake, keepalives
Security DTLS or QUIC's TLS 1.3 integration
Multiple streams per-stream ordering, no global head-of-line blocking

Retransmit or not? Reliable-for-important-things-only: chat messages ACKed and resent, position updates not. Some libraries expose per-message reliability modes (ENet: reliable, unreliable sequenced, unsequenced).

Worked example (FEC). Send 10 data packets plus 2 parity packets (20% overhead). Loss rate 5% random: the chance a group of 12 loses 3 or more is about 2% (binomial); with retransmission-only recovery the receiver would wait a full RTT (50 to 100 ms) on each loss. For a 20 ms-budget audio stream FEC wins.

Production concerns. UDP floods and amplification attacks (DNS, NTP monlist, memcached reflection at 51,000x amplification in the 2018 GitHub 1.35 Tbps attack): spoofed source addresses plus small request / huge reply. Mitigations: don't run open resolvers, rate limit, QUIC address validation and anti-amplification limit (server sends at most 3x the bytes received before the client's address is validated).

Industry examples. WebRTC (RTP/SRTP, ICE, DTLS), Aeron (low-latency messaging in finance), Steam's Game Networking Sockets, Google QUIC (gQUIC) first, then IETF QUIC (RFC 9000).

Decision gravity. Writing a custom reliable-UDP protocol is rarely justified. It becomes a long-lived maintenance burden, and congestion control mistakes harm other users. Use QUIC (library: quiche, msquic, quic-go, ngtcp2) or an established game networking library.

Everyday analogy. Sending postcards but numbering them and asking the recipient to phone for any missing number: you rebuilt a (worse) postal registered-mail service yourself.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting congestion control when "just doing UDP at max rate". Real services are expected to be good network citizens.
  • Using plain UDP across the internet without any security.

notes.title: QUIC: what it is and why
notes.html:
QUIC (RFC 9000, 2021) is a transport protocol built on UDP, carrying TLS 1.3 inside it, and is the transport for HTTP/3. It replaces TCP + TLS and fixes TCP's pain points while running in user space (an app library), so it evolves quickly without OS updates and slips past middleboxes that freeze TCP behaviour (ossification).

Features:

  • 1-RTT connection setup with encryption (transport and TLS handshake combined); 0-RTT on resumption (replay-able data only, so use for idempotent requests).
  • Independent streams: loss on stream A does not block stream B (no TCP head-of-line blocking across HTTP/2 streams).
  • Connection IDs: a connection survives a network change (Wi-Fi to 4G), because identity is not the IP:port 4-tuple. Great for mobile.
  • Encrypted headers and packet numbers: middleboxes see little, which prevents ossification. Packet numbers never repeat (retransmissions get new numbers), removing TCP's retransmit ambiguity.
  • Pluggable congestion control (CUBIC, BBR, per implementation), pacing, built-in ACK ranges and loss detection (RACK-like).
  • Anti-amplification and address validation; minimum client Initial packet 1,200 bytes.
Time to first byte on a new connection (RTT = 100 ms):
HTTP/1.1 or 2 over TCP + TLS 1.3 : 100 (TCP) + 100 (TLS) + 100 (request) = 300 ms
HTTP/3 over QUIC                 : 100 (QUIC+TLS) + 100 (request)       = 200 ms
HTTP/3 with 0-RTT resumption     : 100 (request, sent immediately)      = 100 ms

Worked example (head-of-line blocking). A page loads 30 objects over one HTTP/2 connection. With 2% packet loss, TCP holds ALL streams until the lost segment is retransmitted (100+ ms). With QUIC only the stream with the lost packet waits. Google reported double-digit percentage reductions in search latency and 18% fewer rebuffers for YouTube on QUIC in the poorest networks (confirm exact figures before quoting). Gains are biggest on lossy/high-RTT mobile paths, small on clean fast networks.

curl --http3 -I https://cloudflare-quic.com          # needs curl built with HTTP/3
curl -sI https://www.google.com | grep -i alt-svc
# alt-svc: h3=":443"; ma=2592000     <- server advertises HTTP/3 on UDP 443
nginx -V 2>&1 | grep -o http_v3_module
# nginx.conf (1.25+)
#   listen 443 quic reuseport;
#   listen 443 ssl;
#   add_header Alt-Svc 'h3=":443"; ma=86400';

Discovery: the client first connects with TCP, the server replies Alt-Svc: h3=":443", then the client tries QUIC (also DNS HTTPS records). If UDP is blocked, the client falls back to TCP; tens of percent of enterprise networks historically block or throttle UDP 443.

Costs. QUIC is more CPU-heavy (user space, per-packet crypto, no TSO/GRO offload yet well-supported; UDP GSO helps); UDP may be rate-limited by ISPs; observability tools (tcpdump) cannot see inside, so use qlog/qvis and endpoint logs; load balancers must route by connection ID (Facebook's mvfst/Katran).

Industry examples. Google, Meta (over 75% of its app traffic on QUIC by 2021 per its own engineering blog), Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai, and Netflix/Apple (iOS URLSession uses HTTP/3), Chrome and Firefox enable HTTP/3 by default. Around 30%+ of websites supported HTTP/3 by 2024 per W3Techs/Cloudflare Radar (confirm current).

Decision gravity. Enabling HTTP/3 at your CDN/edge is a low-risk, reversible toggle because clients fall back. Running QUIC end-to-end to backends is a bigger commitment (CPU cost, ops tooling). Choose it for mobile-heavy, high-latency, lossy audiences.

Everyday analogy. TCP is one conveyor belt for all your parcels: one stuck box halts the belt. QUIC gives each parcel type its own belt, in a fast-check-in lane that also remembers you if you change buses mid-trip.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying QUIC is "TCP over UDP" or that it is unreliable. It is reliable, encrypted and congestion-controlled, merely implemented over UDP.
  • Claiming HTTP/3 is always faster. On low-loss networks gains are small and CPU costs higher.
  • Forgetting TCP fallback and the 0-RTT replay risk.

notes.title: Reliability trade-offs: a comparison
notes.html:
Choosing a transport is choosing which costs you accept.

TCP UDP QUIC
Setup RTTs (with TLS 1.3) 2 0 (plain) 1 (0 on resume)
Ordering strict, whole connection none per stream
Loss recovery built in none (DIY) built in, per stream
Congestion control kernel (CUBIC/BBR) none library (CUBIC/BBR)
Head-of-line blocking yes no no across streams
Connection migration no (4-tuple) n/a yes (connection ID)
CPU cost low (offloads) lowest higher (user space, crypto)
Middlebox friendliness high medium (blocked/NAT timeouts short ~30 s) medium (UDP 443 sometimes blocked)
Visible to tcpdump fully fully headers/payload encrypted

Worked example (choosing). A stock-ticker feed pushing 50,000 price updates per second to mobile apps: latest price matters, old ones do not. A QUIC datagram or UDP-with-sequence design, or WebSocket over TCP with conflation (drop stale updates server-side) are options; blindly using TCP means a single lost packet delays every later update by an RTT. A payments API call, however, must use TCP/HTTPS (or HTTP/3) with idempotency keys.

Idempotency matters most. Because of retries (TCP after a timeout, QUIC 0-RTT replay, client retry), any request that can be sent twice must be safe to repeat. Put an idempotency key (Stripe's Idempotency-Key header) on writes.

Observability. Metrics to watch: retransmit rate (TcpRetransSegs / TcpOutSegs, healthy under ~0.5 to 1%), RTT p99, connection setup time, UDP RcvbufErrors (nstat -az UdpRcvbufErrors, ss -uanp with Recv-Q growing = receiver too slow), drops at NIC (ethtool -S).

nstat -az UdpInErrors UdpRcvbufErrors UdpSndbufErrors
sysctl -w net.core.rmem_max=26214400          # bigger UDP receive buffer (e.g. 25 MB)
netstat -su
# Udp: ... 1234 packet receive errors, 1234 receive buffer errors

Industry examples. Cassandra gossip, DNS and StatsD use UDP; Kafka, Postgres use TCP; Google, Meta, Cloudflare move browser-facing traffic to HTTP/3; Slack and Discord use WebSocket (TCP) for chat but UDP for voice.

Decision gravity. Default to TCP/HTTP (or HTTP/3 at the edge) for correctness and tooling; drop to UDP only for provably freshness-critical flows. This choice is moderately hard to reverse once client apps ship, so ship a fallback path.

Everyday analogy. Registered post, normal post and a postcard: pick the cheapest one whose loss you can live with.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing a protocol without saying what loss, order and latency the product can tolerate.
  • Ignoring how much a UDP receive buffer overflow silently drops packets (the app sees nothing).
  • Retrying a non-idempotent write after a timeout.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• UDP: 8-byte header, datagrams, no handshake, ordering, retransmit or congestion control; choose it when freshness beats completeness (games, voice, DNS, telemetry).
  • MTU 1,500; MSS = MTU - 40 (1,460). Avoid fragmentation: use DF + Path MTU Discovery, never block ICMP "frag needed", clamp MSS on tunnels (VPN ~1,400, VXLAN 1,450).
  • PMTUD black holes show as "connects but large transfers hang"; debug with ping -M do -s, tracepath.
  • DIY reliability over UDP needs ordering, ACK/NACK, FEC, congestion control and security; prefer QUIC or a mature library.
  • QUIC = reliable, encrypted, multiplexed transport over UDP: 1-RTT (0-RTT resume), no cross-stream head-of-line blocking, connection migration; costs more CPU and needs TCP fallback; it is the transport for HTTP/3.
  • Pick the transport by tolerance for loss, order and latency; use idempotency keys because retries and 0-RTT can duplicate requests.

questions.promptHtml: What does UDP actually guarantee, and what does it leave to the application?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you know UDP is "TCP minus features" and not just "the fast one".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: UDP gives me ports and a checksum on top of IP, nothing else. Each sendto is one datagram: no connection, no ordering, no retransmission, no congestion control, no flow control. If I need any of those, I build them or pick another protocol.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The UDP header is 8 bytes: src port, dst port, length, checksum. The kernel keeps no per-peer state, so a single socket can talk to many peers and a send never blocks on the peer. Message boundaries are preserved (one send = one recv), unlike TCP's byte stream. Datagrams can be lost, duplicated, reordered or silently dropped when the receive buffer is full.

UDP header (8 B):  | src port 16 | dst port 16 | length 16 | checksum 16 |

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import socket
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
s.bind(("0.0.0.0", 9999))
data, addr = s.recvfrom(2048)   # one datagram, boundaries preserved
s.sendto(b"ack", addr)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying UDP is "unreliable so it is never used for important data" (DNS, QUIC, and most game netcode are UDP).
  • Forgetting that a recv buffer smaller than the datagram truncates it silently.
  • Assuming the checksum protects against corruption end to end in a strong way (it is weak 16-bit).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is the UDP checksum mandatory? -> Optional in IPv4, mandatory in IPv6.
  2. Does UDP preserve message boundaries? -> Yes, one datagram per read.
  3. What happens when the socket receive buffer is full? -> Kernel drops new datagrams; check netstat -su "receive buffer errors".

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer lists "no handshake, faster". The senior adds the absence of congestion control means a UDP app can harm the network, so it must implement its own pacing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A metrics collector dropped 2% of StatsD packets because SO_RCVBUF was the default 208 KB; raising it fixed the gap.

questions.promptHtml: When would you pick UDP over TCP? Give real examples.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests judgment: the right answer is about what failure you tolerate, not speed.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I pick UDP when late data is worthless or when I need control TCP will not give me: live voice/video, game state, DNS lookups, telemetry, and as the base for QUIC. I pick TCP when I need every byte in order and don't want to reimplement reliability.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
TCP gives in-order delivery, so one lost segment stalls everything behind it (head-of-line blocking). For a video call, a retransmitted frame from 300 ms ago is useless; skipping it is better. DNS is one tiny request/response: a handshake would triple the cost, and retry is trivial at app level.

Need Choice
File transfer, DB, REST TCP
Live media, game position UDP
Many tiny request/response UDP (DNS)
Reliable + multiplexed, no HoL QUIC over UDP

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "UDP is faster": throughput on a clean link is similar; the gain is latency and control.
  • Picking UDP to avoid TCP complexity, then rebuilding a worse TCP.
  • Ignoring that corporate firewalls often block UDP other than 53/443.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is DNS UDP? -> One round trip, tiny payload; falls back to TCP when truncated.
  2. Would you stream a file over UDP? -> Only via something like QUIC, which adds reliability.
  3. How do games handle loss? -> Send latest state, drop stale, reliability only for critical events.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "UDP for streaming". Senior: frames it as a choice about retransmission semantics, head-of-line blocking, and who owns congestion control.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team sent chat presence over UDP; NAT timeouts at 30 s killed the flows, forcing keepalives they would have gotten free with TCP.

questions.promptHtml: What is MTU, what is MSS, and how are they related?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Basis for diagnosing "small requests work, big ones hang".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: MTU is the largest IP packet a link can carry, typically 1500 bytes on Ethernet. MSS is the largest TCP payload per segment, so MSS = MTU - 20 (IP) - 20 (TCP) = 1460. Peers announce MSS in the SYN.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
If a packet exceeds the path MTU, a router either fragments it (IPv4, if DF is not set) or drops it and sends ICMP "fragmentation needed" (DF set, and always for IPv6, where routers never fragment). Path MTU Discovery relies on those ICMP messages. Tunnels (VPN, VXLAN, GRE, IPsec) subtract overhead from the MTU, e.g. VXLAN costs about 50 bytes, so inner MTU becomes ~1450.

1500 MTU
 = 20 IP + 20 TCP + 1460 payload (MSS)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking MSS includes headers.
  • Blocking all ICMP on a firewall, which breaks PMTUD.
  • Forgetting that UDP has no MSS; the app must size datagrams (~1200 B is safe, QUIC uses this).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is fragmentation bad? -> Losing one fragment loses the whole datagram, and reassembly costs CPU/memory.
  2. What is MSS clamping? -> A router rewrites the SYN's MSS to fit a tunnel's MTU.
  3. What is jumbo frames' MTU? -> About 9000, needs end-to-end support.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average recites 1500/1460. Senior connects it to tunnels, PMTUD black holes and clamping.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After adding an IPsec tunnel, HTTPS to one partner hung on large responses; MSS clamping to 1360 fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: If you had to add reliability on top of UDP, what mechanisms would you need, and what's the hard part?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows if you understand what TCP actually does and why people rarely should rebuild it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Sequence numbers, ACKs, retransmit timers with RTT estimation, a reorder buffer, flow control, and congestion control. The hard part isn't the ACKs, it's congestion control and loss detection, which decide whether you are a good citizen or melt the network.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Minimum viable design: each packet carries a sequence number; receiver sends cumulative or selective ACKs; sender keeps unacked packets and retransmits on timeout (RTO = smoothed RTT + 4 x variance) or on duplicate/SACK evidence (fast retransmit). Then add a receive window so the sender doesn't overrun the app, and a congestion window (slow start, AIMD, or BBR-style) so it doesn't overrun the network. Optional: FEC to avoid retransmission for latency-critical streams, and per-stream ordering so loss on one stream doesn't block others.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Fixed retransmit timeouts: cause spurious retransmits on slow links and collapse under load.
  • Retransmitting with the same sequence number making RTT sampling ambiguous (Karn's problem); QUIC uses new packet numbers.
  • No pacing: bursts overflow queues.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not just use TCP? -> Need multiple streams without HoL, custom loss policy, or user-space evolution.
  2. How does FEC help? -> Sends parity so small losses recover with no RTT cost, at bandwidth overhead.
  3. How would you test it? -> Linux tc netem loss 5% delay 100ms and compare goodput.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "add sequence numbers and ACKs". Senior names congestion control, RTO estimation, pacing, and notes QUIC already did this properly.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A homegrown UDP file sync saturated a customer's WAN link because it had no congestion control; the network team rate-limited it into uselessness.

questions.contextHtml:
You migrated an API behind a new site-to-site VPN. Health checks (tiny GETs) are green. Users report that uploads and large JSON responses hang forever; small calls are fine. curl -v shows the TLS handshake completing, then the request stalls. The ops team also recently "hardened" the firewall by dropping all ICMP. Tunnel MTU is 1400; hosts use 1500. Red herring: CPU on the gateway is 10%.

$ tcpdump -ni eth0 host 10.2.0.5
12:01:01 10.1.0.9 > 10.2.0.5: Flags [P.], len 1448   (retransmitted x6, no ACK)
12:01:03 10.1.0.9 > 10.2.0.5: Flags [P.], len 1448
questions.promptHtml: What's wrong and how do you fix it without touching every host?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Probably the app is slow or the server is overloaded." Ignores that only large packets fail, and never looks at packet sizes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did it start with the VPN? (timing). Do small and large responses differ in behavior? (size-dependent). Is ICMP blocked? (PMTUD). Is DF set? (likely yes for TCP).
  2. Immediate mitigation: Clamp MSS on the gateway: iptables -t mangle -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: PMTUD black hole (ICMP dropped); app timeout; server overload; TLS issue; asymmetric routing.
  4. How I'd verify each: ping -M do -s 1372 10.2.0.5 succeeds, -s 1400 fails; tcpdump shows 1448-byte segments retransmitting but small ones ACKed; tracepath shows pmtu 1400.
  5. Root cause: Hosts send 1500-byte packets with DF set; the tunnel can carry 1400; the router would send ICMP type 3 code 4, but the firewall drops it, so the sender never shrinks its segments.
  6. Fix: Short term MSS clamp. Long term allow ICMP type 3 code 4 (and ICMPv6 packet-too-big), set tunnel MTU deliberately.
  7. Prevention: Test large-payload paths in pre-prod; firewall baseline that never blocks needed ICMP; synthetic check with 1400-byte payload.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not lower MTU on every host (operational mess); not clear DF (fragmentation hurts).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• UDP (QUIC) traffic also affected? -> Yes; MSS clamp doesn't help UDP, so QUIC stays at ~1200 B payloads or relies on ICMP.
  • IPv6? -> Routers never fragment, so ICMPv6 Packet Too Big is essential.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a payments integration worked for months, then failed only for big batch files after a provider changed to an IPsec link. Everyone suspected the app; one tcpdump showed the same 1448-byte segment retransmitting.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames app/server, no packet-level look.
  • Hire: identifies MTU issue and clamps MSS.
  • Strong hire: explains the PMTUD/ICMP mechanism, covers UDP/IPv6 and a prevention check.

questions.contextHtml:
A StatsD-style metrics ingester receives ~120k UDP packets/s on a 4-core box. Dashboards show gaps; senders report no errors (UDP never does). Network team says the NIC shows no drops. CPU is 60% on one core, others idle.

$ netstat -su
Udp:
    9,884,102 packets received
    412,330 packet receive errors
    RcvbufErrors: 412,330
$ cat /proc/sys/net/core/rmem_max
212992
questions.promptHtml: Why are metrics missing and what would you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "UDP is lossy, that's expected," or blaming the network without checking local counters.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is loss bursty or steady? Single socket? Are senders bursting on flush intervals?
  2. Immediate mitigation: sysctl -w net.core.rmem_max=26214400 and set SO_RCVBUF in the app (the cap applies to the setsockopt value).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Socket buffer overflow (RcvbufErrors counts); single-threaded reader too slow; NIC ring drops; upstream switch drops.
  4. How I'd verify each: nstat -az UdpRcvbufErrors rising during bursts; ss -uamn showing rb full and skmem drops; ethtool -S eth0 | grep drop; top -H showing one hot thread.
  5. Root cause: The kernel buffers incoming datagrams until the app reads; one thread cannot drain bursts so the default ~208 KB buffer overflows and the kernel drops silently.
  6. Fix: Bigger buffer, multiple sockets with SO_REUSEPORT (kernel hashes flows across threads), use recvmmsg for batching.
  7. Prevention: Alert on UdpRcvbufErrors; load test at 3x peak; have senders jitter their flush timers.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not move to TCP blindly (connection counts and blocking producers); big buffers only delay, not fix, a slow consumer.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Hash imbalance with REUSEPORT? -> A hot sender pins one socket; consider BPF steering.
  • Senders behind NAT? -> Source port rewriting is fine for UDP here.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: "missing" metrics for a week traced to one counter nobody graphed. Adding a UdpRcvbufErrors alert caught the next regression in minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "UDP is lossy."
  • Hire: finds buffer overflow and enlarges it.
  • Strong hire: REUSEPORT, recvmmsg, alerting and consumer-speed reasoning.

questions.subtopic: Choosing a protocol for a new product
questions.contextHtml: You're designing a real-time collaborative whiteboard: 50k concurrent rooms, up to 20 users each, cursor positions at 30 Hz, drawing strokes that must never be lost or reordered, and occasional 5 MB image uploads. Users are mostly on mobile networks (3-5% loss, 80-200 ms RTT, frequent Wi-Fi/LTE handoffs). The PM asks "WebSockets or UDP?". Enterprise customers sit behind proxies that often block non-HTTPS traffic.
questions.promptHtml: Which transport(s) would you propose and why?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use UDP for everything because it's real time" or "WebSocket for everything because it's simple," with no split by data type.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How stale can a cursor be? Is stroke order strictly total? What fraction of users are behind proxies? Is there an existing WebRTC/QUIC stack?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design); ship a WebSocket baseline first as it works everywhere.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) All WebSocket/TCP: simple, HoL blocking hurts cursors on lossy mobile; (b) all UDP: needs reliability for strokes; (c) split: reliable ordered channel for strokes, unreliable for cursors; (d) WebTransport / HTTP/3 giving both on one connection.
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype with tc netem loss 4% delay 150ms, measure p99 cursor staleness and stroke latency under each option.
  5. Root cause: Different data have different loss semantics: cursor = latest wins, stroke = must arrive in order.
  6. Fix: WebSocket for strokes and uploads (HTTP upload separately), plus an unreliable channel (WebRTC data channel unordered / WebTransport datagrams) for cursors, with WebSocket fallback when UDP is blocked.
  7. Prevention: Feature flag per transport, metrics on fallback rate and staleness.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not write custom UDP reliability; the operational cost of two paths is real, so keep fallback to WebSocket-only simple.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Mobile handoff? -> QUIC connection migration survives IP changes; TCP does not.
  • Cursor traffic volume? -> 50k x 20 x 30 Hz = 30M msg/s, so server-side fan-out batching/throttling matters more than protocol.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team shipped unreliable cursors and found 90% of users fell back to TCP due to UDP blocking; the "optimization" served a minority.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: single protocol dogma.
  • Hire: splits data by reliability need, includes fallback.
  • Strong hire: quantifies fan-out, mentions QUIC/WebTransport migration and test plan under loss.

questions.contextHtml:
Your public UDP service (a game-lobby discovery endpoint) suddenly shows 8 Gbps outbound with only 200 Mbps inbound. Your transit provider threatens to null-route your IP. Requests are 40 bytes and responses are 1,200 bytes. Source IPs in the logs are from all over the world, including residential ranges that don't play your game.

$ tcpdump -ni eth0 udp port 27015 -c 3
IP 203.0.113.7.4444 > 192.0.2.10.27015: UDP, length 40
IP 192.0.2.10.27015 > 203.0.113.7.4444: UDP, length 1200
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and how do you stop it permanently?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blocks the offending IPs one by one, not realizing the sources are spoofed victims.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the response bigger than the request? Are source IPs victims or real clients? Is there any auth in the request?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Rate-limit responses per source IP, temporarily drop the lobby response size, or geo/ACL-limit while patching.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Reflection/amplification attack (spoofed source); legitimate traffic spike; misconfigured client loop; our server is replying to broadcast.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare packet ratios (30x amplification); check that "clients" never send follow-up traffic; sample sources against known victim reports.
  5. Root cause: UDP has no handshake, so an attacker spoofs the victim's IP in a 40-byte request and my server sends 1,200 bytes to the victim: amplification factor 30.
  6. Fix: Short term: per-IP rate limit and response caps. Long term: require a stateless cookie/challenge so the first reply is no larger than the request (QUIC's anti-amplification 3x rule), shrink responses, require a token.
  7. Prevention: Ratio alerts on egress/ingress, BCP38 ingress filtering requests to upstream, load tests for response-size/request-size.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not block by IP blindly (hits victims); a challenge adds one RTT to discovery.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why do DNS/NTP/memcached get abused the same way? -> Same mechanism: small request, large reply, no source validation.
  • Can TCP be used this way? -> Much less, since the handshake validates the source.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a debug UDP stats endpoint left on the internet became a reflector overnight; the fix was a one-line bind to the private interface.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: IP blocking only.
  • Hire: names reflection and rate-limits.
  • Strong hire: stateless cookie challenge, 3x rule, egress/ingress ratio alerting.

questions.promptHtml: Why was QUIC built on UDP instead of being a new transport protocol, and what does it fix over TCP+TLS?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand ossification and head-of-line blocking, not just "HTTP/3 is faster".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: New IP protocols get dropped by middleboxes and TCP lives in kernels, so evolving it takes years. QUIC runs in user space over UDP, which every network passes. It combines the transport and TLS 1.3 handshake in 1 RTT (0-RTT on resumption), has independent streams so one loss doesn't stall the rest, and connection IDs so connections survive IP changes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
TCP+TLS1.3 needs 1 RTT for TCP plus 1 for TLS = 2 RTT before data; QUIC needs 1 (0 for resumption). HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection, but TCP delivers bytes in order, so one lost packet blocks all streams. QUIC makes loss recovery per stream. Packets are encrypted including most header fields, preventing middleboxes from depending on them. Connections are identified by a connection ID, not the 4-tuple, enabling migration from Wi-Fi to LTE.

TCP+TLS1.3: SYN -> SYN/ACK -> ACK+ClientHello -> ServerHello... -> data   (~2 RTT)
QUIC:       Initial(ClientHello) -> Initial+Handshake -> data              (1 RTT)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming QUIC removes all head-of-line blocking (it removes it across streams, not inside a stream).
  • Forgetting 0-RTT data is replayable, so only idempotent requests.
  • Assuming UDP is always allowed; some networks block 443/UDP, so clients fall back to TCP.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is connection migration? -> Same connection ID continues after the client's IP/port changes.
  2. Is QUIC always faster? -> Not on clean, low-latency links; user-space CPU cost is higher.
  3. How does QUIC avoid being an amplification vector? -> Server sends at most 3x bytes before validating the client address.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "faster, uses UDP". Senior: ossification, per-stream loss recovery, migration, replay risk of 0-RTT, CPU cost and fallback strategy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A CDN rollout of HTTP/3 improved p95 on mobile but raised CPU 15% because UDP offload (GSO) was not enabled on the servers.

questions.promptHtml: Compare TCP, UDP and QUIC on ordering, loss recovery, congestion control and head-of-line blocking. How do you decide?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Wants a decision framework, not three memorized definitions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: TCP: reliable, ordered byte stream, kernel congestion control, HoL blocking across the whole connection. UDP: nothing, you own everything. QUIC: reliable per stream, ordering only within a stream, built-in congestion control in user space, encrypted. I choose by what loss means for the data and who I want to own the logic.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Property TCP UDP QUIC
Reliability yes no yes (per stream)
Ordering whole conn none per stream
Setup RTT 1 (+TLS 1-2) 0 1 / 0
Congestion ctl kernel none user space, pluggable
Middlebox friendly yes mostly UDP 443, sometimes blocked
Evolvability slow (kernel) n/a fast (app update)

Decision: all bytes must arrive and I don't care about HoL: TCP. Stale data is worthless: UDP with app logic. Many independent streams, mobile clients, want fast evolution: QUIC. Cost to remember: reliability costs latency exactly when loss happens (one RTT for retransmit).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating "unreliable" as "no feedback"; real-time protocols still need loss feedback for rate adaptation.
  • Ignoring operational support: debugging encrypted QUIC with tcpdump is harder.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does TCP's HoL actually hurt? -> HTTP/2 with 1-3% loss on mobile.
  2. Can I mix reliability levels? -> QUIC datagram extension, SCTP partial reliability, WebRTC data channels.
  3. What does a retransmit cost at 150 ms RTT? -> At least 150 ms (or less with fast retransmit after 3 dup ACKs), added to tail latency.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists features. Senior argues from loss semantics, tail latency, observability and fallback cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team moved telemetry to QUIC and lost tcpdump visibility; they had to add qlog and endpoint metrics first.

questions.contextHtml: You enabled HTTP/3 (alt-svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400) on your CDN edge. Metrics after 24 h: overall p50 latency improved 8%, but p99 got worse by 12%, and 6% of requests show "protocol=h2" despite alt-svc advertisement. A large enterprise customer reports intermittent 5 s delays on first page load. Edge CPU rose from 35% to 48%. Red herring: origin latency is flat.
questions.promptHtml: What do you investigate, and do you keep HTTP/3 on?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "HTTP/3 is faster, so roll back since numbers are mixed," or "ignore p99".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 5 s delay on new connections? Which networks? Do affected users sit behind corporate firewalls? Is p99 segmented by protocol?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove alt-svc for the affected ASN/customer, or shorten ma, leaving others on h3.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: UDP blocked or throttled so client tries QUIC, times out, then falls back to TCP (the 5 s is a fallback timer); UDP not GSO-offloaded raising CPU; middlebox rate limiting UDP; cohort shift in p99 (mobile users now counted).
  4. How I'd verify each: Split latency by protocol and by ASN; Chrome net-export; check client fallback rate; perf top for UDP send path; ethtool -k for tx-udp-segmentation.
  5. Root cause: Clients that learned alt-svc attempt QUIC first (or race it), and on UDP-hostile networks pay the fallback delay; CPU rise is user-space packet processing without offload.
  6. Fix: Enable UDP GSO/GRO, keep h3 but exclude hostile networks, rely on client racing (happy eyeballs) and shorter alt-svc caching for the pilot.
  7. Prevention: Staged rollout by percentage, dashboards segmented by protocol/ASN, fallback-rate alert.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not turn off h3 globally for a cohort problem; not trust aggregate p50.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Is 0-RTT worth enabling? -> Only for idempotent GETs due to replay.
  • Load balancer ECMP breaking connections? -> Needs connection-ID-aware routing (QUIC-LB).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a hotel Wi-Fi blocking UDP/443 explained 80% of complaints; the "slow" users were all on a handful of ASNs.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: all-or-nothing rollback.
  • Hire: segments by protocol and finds fallback delay.
  • Strong hire: GSO, ECMP/CID routing, staged rollout and metrics plan.

questions.contextHtml:
Your in-app voice calls (UDP, 20 ms Opus frames, 50 packets/s) get complaints in emerging markets: robotic audio, 4-6% loss, RTT 250 ms, jitter 80 ms. The team proposes "just retransmit lost packets" and separately "move audio to TCP for reliability". Bandwidth per call is 32 kbps; users are on metered data.

rtp stats: loss=5.1% jitter=82ms rtt=251ms concealed_samples=14%
questions.promptHtml: Evaluate the two proposals and suggest what to do.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks TCP because "it's reliable", ignoring that retransmitted audio arrives after the playout deadline.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is loss random or bursty? Mouth-to-ear budget (~150-250 ms)? Is video also sent? Are costs per MB?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Enable Opus in-band FEC and DTX; tune jitter buffer adaptively.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Burst loss exceeding PLC ability; jitter buffer too small; sender bitrate too high for link; poor Wi-Fi.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log loss run lengths; compare concealed samples vs jitter-buffer size; test with tc netem loss 5% delay 125ms 40ms.
  5. Root cause: With 250 ms RTT, a retransmit arrives 250+ ms after loss, beyond the playout deadline, so it is wasted bandwidth. TCP would stall the whole stream behind a lost packet (HoL), giving freezes then bursts.
  6. Fix: FEC (Opus LBRR, or RED redundancy), bounded-delay NACK only for video keyframes, adaptive bitrate from RTCP feedback, dynamic jitter buffer.
  7. Prevention: Call quality metrics (MOS estimate) per region, a netem-based CI test.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: FEC raises bandwidth by 20-50%, which costs metered users; pick the level adaptively. Don't use TCP for media.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Bursty loss defeats FEC? -> Interleave or add redundancy depth, at latency cost.
  • Why is NACK fine for video? -> Keyframe loss makes whole GOP useless; worth the delay.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: the team ran A/B tests of FEC levels per country and found 2x redundancy helped India but hurt metered users in Brazil.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: chooses TCP/retransmit.
  • Hire: FEC and jitter buffer reasoning.
  • Strong hire: deadline math, adaptive redundancy, cost trade-off with test plan.

questions.subtopic: Spot the bug in a UDP sender
questions.contextHtml:
A telemetry client sends batches of events as one UDP datagram per batch. After a feature added more fields, a few customers on VPNs report missing data while most work. Review this code. The server logs show no errors. Packet capture shows IP fragments from this host, and none of the fragments arrive at the server for the failing customers.

import socket, json
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
def flush(events):
    payload = json.dumps(events).encode()      # grows with batch size
    s.sendto(payload, ("telemetry.example.com", 8125))
    events.clear()
questions.promptHtml: What's the bug, why do only some customers fail, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "UDP is unreliable, add retries." Doesn't see the datagram-size issue.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Typical and max payload size? Which networks fail? Are fragments dropped by a firewall?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap batch size to ~1200 bytes of payload.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Fragmented datagrams dropped by firewalls/NAT (they filter non-first fragments); loss of any fragment loses all; PMTU lower on VPNs; server buffer too small.
  4. How I'd verify each: ping -M do -s 1372; tcpdump ip[6:2] & 0x3fff != 0 to see fragments; compare payload size distribution with failing customers.
  5. Root cause: Payloads above ~1472 bytes (1500 - 20 IP - 8 UDP) are fragmented; on VPNs the MTU is smaller so more fragments, and many networks drop fragments, so the entire datagram vanishes. Fragmented loss probability multiplies per fragment.
  6. Fix: Split into multiple datagrams under ~1200 bytes each, with a batch sequence number so the server can detect gaps; or send large batches over TCP/HTTPS.
  7. Prevention: Assert on payload size; test through a 1400-MTU path; alert on missing sequence numbers.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rely on IP fragmentation; not set DF and ignore the EMSGSIZE error.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• IPv6 behavior? -> No router fragmentation; the sender must size to path MTU.
  • What size is safe? -> About 1200 B is the QUIC-style conservative bound; verify for your paths.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: telemetry dropped 100% for one big customer for weeks because their firewall dropped non-initial fragments.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds retries.
  • Hire: identifies fragmentation and caps size.
  • Strong hire: explains fragment loss math, sequence numbers and TCP alternative.

questions.contextHtml: A teammate proposes replacing gRPC/TCP between services with a custom UDP protocol "to cut latency" for a hot path doing 200k small RPCs/s inside one datacenter (RTT 0.2 ms, loss ~0.001%). Current p99 is 6 ms, p50 1.2 ms. Profiling shows 40% of time in TLS and serialization, 10% in kernel TCP. There is no written SLO, only "make it faster". Mixed replies include a Kubernetes service mesh sidecar adding ~1 ms per hop.
questions.promptHtml: How do you respond to the proposal?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Either "UDP is faster, go ahead" or an outright "no" with no data.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What's the target latency and who feels it? What fraction of p99 is network vs queuing vs GC? Is the sidecar required? Can calls be idempotent?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None; ask for an SLO and a profile first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Latency is dominated by sidecar, serialization, TLS and queueing, not TCP; p99 tail from GC or retransmit timeouts (min RTO 200 ms would show as spikes, not 6 ms); connection setup churn; Nagle/delayed ACK interactions.
  4. How I'd verify each: Flame graph (perf, async-profiler); ss -ti for retransmits and RTT; trace spans per hop; check TCP_NODELAY; connection reuse.
  5. Root cause: Kernel TCP is 10% of cost; at 0.001% loss HoL hardly matters. A UDP rewrite would save at most a few percent while taking on reliability, congestion and security.
  6. Fix: Cheaper wins: connection pooling, TCP_NODELAY, drop the sidecar hop or use eBPF/mTLS offload, binary serialization, batch RPCs. If still needed, consider QUIC libraries rather than custom.
  7. Prevention: Written latency SLOs, perf budgets per hop, a benchmark harness.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not write a protocol for a 10% gain; custom reliability brings correctness risk, no tooling, and poor debuggability.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if loss rose to 1%? -> TCP retransmits spike tail latency; reevaluate, and QUIC might help.
  • Kernel bypass (DPDK)? -> Only at much higher scale, with dedicated engineering.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a similar proposal died after a flame graph showed JSON serialization at 35%; switching format beat the whole UDP plan.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: yes/no without data.
  • Hire: asks for profile and SLO.
  • Strong hire: quantifies upside bound, offers cheaper wins and explicit risks.
